extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, judges, law students, and inventors drafting or litigating patents
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the statutory and judicial requirements for a patent specification (what must be described, how it limits the patent, how courts and juries evaluate sufficiency and construction), plus rules on patent renewal/extension. Applicable to preparing, interpreting, and litigating U.S. patent specifications and renewals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description and enablement requirement (Act of July 4, 1836, §6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before any inventor shall receive a patent ... he shall deliver a written description of his invention or discovery, and of the manner and process of making, constructing, using and compounding the same, in such full, clear, and exact terms, avoiding unnecessary prolixity, as to enable any person skilled in the art or science to which it appertains ... to make, construct, compound, and use the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For machines: 'he shall fully explain the principle and the several modes in which he has contemplated the application of that principle ... and shall particularly specify and point out the part, improvement, or combination, which he claims as his own invention or discovery.' Accompany the description with drawings/written references where applicable, or with specimens for compositions of matter; descriptions and drawings to be signed by the inventor and attested by two witnesses; furnish a model where a representation by model is possible. The description must enable a person skilled in the art to make and use the invention from the specification itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification forms part of the patent and controls construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Under U.S. law the specification is drawn up and filed before the patent and is referred to in the patent itself; the patent and specification are to be construed together, and the specification may control the generality of the terms of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawings annexed to the specification form a part of it and are to be regarded in construing the whole instrument; where specification and patent terms differ, the specification can limit or explain broad patent language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court determines construction; jury decides factual sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the province of the court to determine what is intended to be patented and whether the patent is valid in point of law; whether the invention is specifically described with reasonable certainty is a question of law for the court. It is the province of the jury to decide, on evidence of experts, whether the invention is described in such full, clear, and exact terms as to enable a skilful person to put it in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court gives the construction of the patent (absolutely if no terms of art or surrounding circumstances require evidence; conditionally if such matters exist). Where terms of art or surrounding circumstances affect meaning, those facts are for the jury based on expert testimony. Use experts to show enablement to a skilled artisan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification may control generality but repugnancy voids the patent
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule allowing the letters-patent to be controlled by the specification cannot extend to a case where the terms of the former are inconsistent with those of the latter; if there is a clear repugnancy between the description of the invention in the specification and the invention stated in the letters-patent, the patent will be void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the patent issues for an invention not described in the specification, the statute is not complied with; the specification cannot be used to justify a patent that claims something different from what is described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents construed liberally to ascertain nature and extent of claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents are to be construed liberally and not subjected to a rigid interpretation; the nature and extent of the invention claimed is to be ascertained from the fair sense of the words employed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While courts take a liberal view to give effect to inventor's rights and promote useful arts, liberal construction is balanced against statutory requisites that protect the public. Do not rely on overly technical narrow reading when the claim's nature is otherwise apparent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two primary objectives of a specification
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification has two objects: (1) to make known the manner of constructing the machine (if a machine) so as to enable artisans to make and use it after expiration; (2) to put the public in possession of what the party claims as his own invention so as to ascertain if he claims anything already known and to warn innocent purchasers or users of potential infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft the specification both to enable post-expiration practice and to clearly notify the public of the patentee's claim boundaries to avoid misleading or overbroad claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe the subject-matter claimed with reasonable certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: To describe the subject-matter, or what the patentee claims to have invented, so as to enable the public to know what his claim is. It must appear with reasonable certainty what the party intends to claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Language need not be highly technical but must not mislead; the whole specification should be read in connection (words standing alone not singled out). If the claim is left ambiguous or uncertain so that the court cannot, without conjecture, gather the invention, the patent is void. Use clear statements and, where possible, explicit claim language or specific pointing-out of claimed parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish clearly between what is old and what is new
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute requires the patentee to give a written description which involves, where the patentee uses what is old, distinguishing between what is old and what is new; he is required to point out in what his invention or discovery consists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the description mixes old and new without showing the patentee does not claim the old parts, the patent may be broader than the invention and therefore void. Be explicit about prior art and the novel contributions; identify which parts are admitted old and which parts are claimed as new.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement patents must state specifically what the improvement is and be limited to it
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patent be for an improved machine, or for an improvement of a machine, it must state in what the improvement specifically consists, and it must be limited to such improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A general statement that the machine is 'an improvement' without stating particulars is insufficient and can render the patent void for ambiguity. Clearly define the improvement and limit claims to that improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cannot include pre-existing (not-new) matter in claim — if any claimed part is not new, patent is void
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever appears to be covered by the claim of the patentee as his own invention must be taken as part of the claim; courts cannot reject any part of the claim; and therefore if it turns out that anything claimed is not new, the patent is void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not claim old elements as if they were novel; ensure claims are supported by specification and avoid claiming the exclusive use of known machinery. If a claimed element is shown not to be new, the entire patent claim may be invalidated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must enable public to practise invention after patent expiration
rubrics_metrics.description: One object of the specification is to enable artisans to make and use the invention at the expiration of the patent, giving the public the full benefit of the discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include sufficient detail, drawings, modes of application, and examples so that a skilled person could reproduce and practice the invention without undue experimentation after term expiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Renewal/extension requirements and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: The eighteenth section authorizes the renewal of patents in all cases where the board of commissioners is satisfied of the usefulness of the invention, and of the inadequacy of remuneration to the patentee. Inventions of merit only are the subject of the new grant; such as have had the public confidence ... 'that no extension of the patent shall be granted after the expiration of the term for which it was originally issued.' 'And the benefit of such renewal shall extend to assignees and grantees of the right to use the thing patented, to the extent of their respective interests therein.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Renewals/extensions must be sought before original patent expiration; they are available only for useful inventions where remuneration was inadequate; extensions restore the exclusive rights but will be qualified to protect assignees/grantees who were using patented articles at time of renewal (their rights extend only to their respective interests). Consider public reliance and purchasers' protections when construing renewal provisions.
